title: Full from full: the peace chant
hook: the chant that ends om shanti: take the full from the full, and the full remains
carry: that is full, and this world is full too
tomorrow: the teacher's charge to the student: "speak the truth, practice dharma"

segments.voice: Yesterday: neti, neti, neti neti: the self is beyond every name, and Yajnavalkya finally went away. Your line was neti neti: the self is beyond every name.

Light a candle, and use it to light a second one. Look at the first flame: it hasn't gotten any smaller. Something was given away completely, and nothing was lost. At a Hindu gathering, a yoga class, or the start of an Upanishad recital, you may have heard a short Sanskrit chant that ends om shanti, shanti, shanti. It comes from the opening of the Brihadaranyaka's fifth book, and it's where this path leaves the book.
screen: `A CANDLE LIGHTS A CANDLE.` → `THE FIRST FLAME LOSES NOTHING.` → `A CHANT HEARD AT THE START OF STUDY.`

segments.voice: Here it is. Purnam adah purnam idam purnat purnam udacyate, purnasya purnam adaya purnam evavashishyate. That is full. This is full. From the full, the full comes forth. Take the full from the full, and the full alone remains. Purna means full, whole, complete, lacking nothing. That is the far side, Brahman beyond everything you can point to. This is the near side, the world right here, the one you're sitting in. And the chant refuses to make either one the lesser half. The world doesn't come out of Brahman like a slice out of a cake, leaving a hole. It comes out like a flame from a flame. The tradition attaches it as the peace chant of the Isha Upanishad, too, and it's chanted at the start of study, worship and gatherings. And it's a fitting place to finish the Brihadaranyaka, because of a woman you met in it. Yajnavalkya was about to leave home, and offered to settle his property between his two wives. Maitreyi asked one question: if this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? No, he said; you'd live the way rich people live. Then what would I do with it, she said. Tell me what you know. She wanted the whole, not a bigger piece. Set her question beside this chant and you can hear an answer. Brahman, the whole, doesn't shrink when the world comes forth, and the world that comes forth isn't a scrap. That is full, and this, right here, is full. Tomorrow, a new Upanishad, the Taittiriya, and a teacher's speech to his graduating students.
screen: `THAT IS FULL. THIS IS FULL.` · `A FLAME FROM A FLAME, NOT A SLICE.` · `THE PEACE CHANT OF STUDY AND WORSHIP.` · `MAITREYI: WOULD THE EARTH'S WEALTH MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` · then, large: `FULL FROM FULL.`

segments.voice: On the in-breath, let the word come: full; on the out-breath: full. See whether the breath you just gave away left you lacking anything, with the next one already arriving. If you like, say the chant silently, or just its first line, purnam adah, purnam idam, and let the words and the breath move together until the words fall away.
Purna, full, whole, complete. In the peace chant, what that is, what this is, and what remains when the full is taken from the full.
Your line: that is full, and this world is full too. Not a slice taken out of Brahman. Rest well.

howItsDone: The purnam adah chant is recited as the shanti mantra of the Isha Upanishad and of the Shukla Yajurveda tradition, at the start and end of study, at pujas and at many gatherings, followed by om shanti, shanti, shanti.

chat.meaning: Purna means full. That, Brahman, is full; this, the world, is full; the world comes forth from the full like a flame from a flame, and the full remains.

tie.story: Maitreyi turned down the earth's wealth to ask for the whole, and the book closes chanting: that is full, this is full.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Sam the chant says the world in front of them comes from the full and is full too, like a flame lit from a flame.
tie.you: where do you feel like a piece instead of whole?
